publications.title: Inferring Agenda: An Unsupervised Approach to SCOTUS Issue Classification
publications.subtitle: The Ohio State University
publications.description: This project presents an end-to-end machine learning pipeline to process, embed, and cluster large-scale legal text data, addressing computational efficiency and interpretability challenges present in high-dimensional natural language data. The goal is to analyze judicial behavior at the petition stage of the U.S. Supreme Court by classifying legal texts into issue areas based on the SPAETH Supreme Court database, a widely used dataset that codes Supreme Court decisions by various characteristics, including legal issue area. A key limitation, though, is that only accepted petitions are labeled with a SPAETH category. To understand the topic distribution among all petitions, consensus clustering was employed on the full set of petitions to infer clusters that approximate SPAETH issue areas. This was preferable over supervised learning because supervised methods would rely on training a classifier on accepted petitions and then applying it on unaccepted petitions; however, this strategy would introduce a sampling bias because the training sample would not be random. We can use the resulting clusters to determine the semantic content of a petition, thus enabling us to compare what the Supreme Court is asked to hear vs. what they actually hear. The Supreme Court can unilaterally strip and provide rights to people, but, until now, the factors regarding case selection were a mystery. This research offers a data-driven framework to provide critical insights into whose voices are amplified, whose are silenced, and how the Supreme Court steers national policy.

I am beyond excited to announce that upon my graduation from The Ohio State University in May, I will be pursuing my Master of Engineering (M.Eng.) in Computer Science at Cornell University . There, I will be focusing on computing systems. I'm looking forward to working at the intersection of hardware and software, and learning how to architect reliable, scalable systems that can handle real-world demands efficiently. This was not an easy decision by any means, as I was also accepted into other prestigious computer science programs such as Columbia University , Georgia Institute of Technology , The University of Texas at Austin , and University of Southern California , and I had a full-time offer on the table from American Honda Motor Company, Inc. In the end, I decided to pursue graduate education at Cornell University because the collaborative engineering culture and the opportunity to learn from world-class faculty made it feel like the best place to challenge myself in order to maximize learning and growth, thus laying a strong foundation for long-term career success. I want to extend a massive thank you to every mentor I've had thus far. Each one of you has pushed me to become a better version of myself and I'm incredibly grateful. An extra special thank you to Janet Box-Steffensmeier , Joe Bewley , and Spyros Blanas for your continuous support and guidance as letter writers and mentors throughout this grad application cycle. I also want to sincerely thank everyone I've worked with at Mimecast , NetJets , American Honda Motor Company, Inc. , and American Institutions & Methodology Lab for equipping me with the tools I need to succeed in this next chapter. And finally, I want to thank my friends and family whose support and confidence in me never wavered. Especially Ramya Rajasekhar, Shash Rajashekara , and Abhav Rajashekara , I could never have gotten here without you guys❤️. I can't wait to join such an inspiring and uplifting community in Ithaca. I'm looking forward to diving into my studies, building projects, connecting with my peers, and seeing what the future holds! 🌰➡️🐻 #CornellUniversity #CornellBound #IvyLeague #ComputerScience #Engineering

Exciting news. We're No. 1251 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list! But the number isn't the story. We grew because of the problem we're solving and how we're solving it. The story is what happens to your resume after you hit submit. It doesn't usually get rejected. Rejection would be a response - and I know from my many job searches, a response is sometimes too much to ask:(. Instead the resume gets uploaded to an S3 bucket in a data center in Northern Virginia. Encrypted at rest. Replicated across three availability zones. Amazon guarantees it eleven nines of durability (Azure is probably similar), which means your resume is statistically more likely to survive the next century than most governments (dependent on data retention policies:)). What a journey your lonely resume gets to be a part of. It is safe. It is indexed. It is beautifully preserved. It has simply never been read by a person. That's not cruelty. That's one person with 400 applications and nine days. And all the tools do is match words on pieces of digital paper (four clusters generally matched between resume and JD). We fixed the silence. We allowed our customers to talk to and interview all candidates in real-time. Finding the best fit NOW, while building pipeline for the next role. Thank you to our customers, our partners, and the team that built this while I was busy writing Linkedin posts. Congrats to everyone else on the list. Aiming for the top 500 next year! Learn more here: https://lnkd.in/gX966C9V .

As I wrap up my internship, I have been reflecting on how much I have grown since my first day. I came into this experience curious about how electronics could play such an important role in controlling an engine of this scale. As the weeks went by, I gradually learned how electronic control modules, or ECMs, are developed and tested. I gained hands-on experience with ECM hardware and printed circuit boards, including the opportunity to develop an embedded solution for one of the board’s components. I also analyzed engineering test data, which showed me how test results can guide design improvements. Working alongside experienced engineers showed me that unexpected results are often where the most valuable learning begins. Those moments taught me to slow down, ask better questions, and look at a problem from a different perspective before reaching a conclusion. I could not have had this meaningful experience without the support of my team. I would especially like to thank my manager, Cheryl Steffel Verbeke , for making my internship such a smooth and rewarding experience. I am also grateful to my supervisor, Andres A. Mena , for his guidance throughout my engineering projects, and to Aun Abbas for being a great mentor along the way. I could not have asked for a better opportunity to learn, contribute, and grow as an engineer with Caterpillar Inc.
